Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of his statement yesterday that in the reassessment of defence policy the government is considering the kind, quality and number of armaments that we will want to commit to
NORAD. In light of this, will the Prime Minister say whether, as a result of the agreement signed last March, Canada considers itself committed to participate in NORAD until May 12, 1973?

Mr. Speaker, NORAD is a control device. It is not one to which any specific number of men, arms or materiel are committed. Each of the members of NORAD decides the input that it will place at NORAD's disposal. The agreement can exist essentially with very little arms from one side or the other. We are a member of NORAD. We have renewed that agreement. The number and kind of armaments put at the disposal of NORAD on the Canadian side is a decision for the Canadian government.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether Canada's continuation in or withdrawal from the NORAD agreement prior to 1973 is one of the matters under examination in the review of defence and foreign policy. My question is directed not to what arms might be provided but to whether we would stay in or withdraw from the agreement itself. Is this question under review?
Well, Mr. Speaker, if we decided to withdraw our arms at the disposition of NORAD, technically we could stay in the agreement but it would be of very little avail.
It would be a breach of agreement.

That is why I am indicating that from our point of view the crucial matter is the amount of arms we want to put at the disposition of NORAD. If, as I said, it were practically nil, I suppose that under this hypothesis the agreement would become defunct.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Then it would perhaps be correct to say that the continuation in or withdrawal from NORAD itself prior to 1973 is a matter that comes within the terms of the reassessment and review?

Yes, indirectly, Mr. Speaker. Once again I am looking at the hypothesis that we would put no arms there. Then you could say the agreement is continued but there is nothing in it. Mr. Chairman, on Thursday, November 14, I was participating in this debate. At that time I said that when one considers the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, commonly known as the Kennedy round, one thinks of the words fait accompli
November 19, 19G8

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

I was saying, Mr. Chairman, that when one considers the effect of the Kennedy round negotiations one finds no substantial reduction in effective protection resulting therefrom. In some cases there is higher protection than there was before. This has been the finding of the Economic Council of Canada which made a detailed study of the Kennedy round recommendations. They found that there was no reduction in effective protection as a result of these negotiations.
One of the recommendations the Economic Council of Canada made was that there should be an accelerated reduction of tariffs as one way of dealing with persistent price and cost increases in Canada. This recommendation was rejected by the Prime Minister in his statement on September 12, and has been rejected by the Minister of Finance in his recent budget. The approach of the Minister of Finance to the handling of the price and cost increases we are experiencing in Canada has been to create a slack economy, to create more unemployment. This is contrary to one of the methods recommended by the Economic Council of Canada.
I said on that evening that Canada must have a free trade policy in order to develop her economic and productive strength. The experience Canadians have had has been that restrictions have been imposed by the government which have hindered the development of a real free trade policy for Canada. One of the major restrictions in this regard has been our monetary policy. I stated that our policy with regard to a fixed exchange rate and our attitude and policy regarding foreign exchange reserves have created restrictions on the development of a free trade policy. I quoted extensively from statements made by the present Postmaster General to develop this point. Since many people believe that when we in the New Democratic party set forth a principle that principle is not regarded as having any validity by the people in government, I am going to quote again
Ways and Means
from what the present Postmaster General said back in 1967. I should like to refer to an article he wrote entitled, "The Nation Keepers", in which he referred to foreign guide lines to Canada's economic future. At page 214 the author develops the principle that Canada should have an aggressive trade policy and states:
If Canada pursues an aggressive free trade policy it is obvious that our fixed exchange rate policy will not work. We will have to go through so many fundamental changes in industrial organization that only a freely moving rate will be able to adjust to the productive process and measure our success or failure in achieving our aims. As J. E. Meade has written, there is no choice for free traders. "Free trade and fixed exchange rates are incompatible in the modern world." This is particularly true for Canada which depends on trade, has a heavily protected manufacturing industry, and is much affected by the slightest changes in the economic policy of its neighbour. Free trade will bring a more efficient use of our resources and expand our possibilities of growth, but these changes cannot possibly work their way through the economy within the constraints of a fixed rate.
These statements were made by the present Postmaster General, and I have yet to hear a government spokesman, including the present Postmaster General, give any forward push to these very necessary principles with regard to the foreign exchange rate policy or foreign exchange reserves. We in the New Democratic party have advocated this principle for quite some time. When we have the Postmaster General enunciating the same principle, when we have the Financial Times of September 23 setting forth the necessity of solving this problem, when on November 14 we have the president of the Royal Bank, Mr. Earl McLaughlin, stating that the exchange rate policy and the foreign exchange reserves are imposing restrictions with regard to free trade, one would hope that the government would take immediate action to achieve the release of these restrictions and have a more definite free trade policy.
The second proposition I set forth last week was that we should examine the industrial structure of our Canadian economy. This, of course, necessitates an in-depth study of foreign ownership in Canada. It was for this reason the Watkins committee made a thorough study of foreign ownership and structure in the Canadian economy. The report to this committee states that in 1964 we had $27 billion of foreign investment, 86 per cent of which was United States investment; 12 per cent investment from the United Kingdom and 8 per cent from other countries. I understand that a projection of the $27 billion in

November 19, 19S8
Ways and Means
1964 reveals that the figure is now close to $35 billion. When one reads that in certain industries such as automobile parts and rubber United States investment is 97 per cent, that in chemical products there is 78 per cent control, that in electrical apparatus there is 77 per cent control, one can appreciate the impact of foreign investment in Canada.
It was for this reason the Watkins committee went into such a detailed study concerning the problems of extraterritoriality, branch operations in Canada and multi-national corporations, and an effort was made to determine just what penetration had been made in these particular areas. Mr. Watkins, who was the chairman of this committee on foreign ownership, in an article written for a magazine called Executive in August of 1968 set forth his views concerning foreign investment. At this stage one is not complaining about the general problem of foreign investment because we in Canada invite foreign investment. However, one has to look at the penetration that has been made and the consequences that may follow this domination of our Canadian industry. Mr. Watkins said:
The amount of foreign investment, or foreign ownership, is not an issue in and of itself. There is no virtue in trying to minimize it for its own sake. I suspect that most people in this audience would readily agree with that proposition. If so, you ought also to agree that neither is there any virtue in trying to maximize the level of foreign ownership in Canada for its own sake. Unfortunately, some important groups in this country at least give the appearance of having fallen victim to the latter fallacy.
Then he sets forth just what the approach of Canada should be.
What we should want is to maximize the net benefits from foreign investments, in order to have as large benefits as possible, by increasing benefits and decreasing costs. Basically, this means using public policy to increase the economic benefits and decrease the political costs from foreign ownership. It means using foreign investment in such a way as to get the largest possible increase in the standard of living for Canadians, and to get the smallest possible reduction in our sovereignty and our economic and political independence.
I am sure that Canadians would agree with the ultimate goal for which we are striving with regard to the part foreign ownership should play in the Canadian economy. This is why the Watkins report recommended tariff reductions so as to increase economic benefits from foreign investment. As Mr. Watkins says, Mr. Chairman:
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Tariff reduction is not a universal panacea to solve all our problems, as some of my colleagues

in economics seem sometimes to imply, and it might well exacerbate some of these problems. The structure of Canadian industry is frequently one of too many and too small firms. There is a need for fewer and larger firms, or rationalization.! Tariff reduction, by permitting import competition, provides a spur for rationalization and some protection for the consumer after rationalization, but it does not in itself provide the means for rationalization. There remains a need for capital, for leadership, for planning.
This is why the Canadian economy must face the problem of extraterritoriality. The approach of the Watkins report to this problem is this:
The actual problems of extraterritoriality arise for Canada from the intrusion of United States law via the medium of the American-controlled subsidiary resident in Canada with respect to trade with certain Community countries, with respect to compliance with the decrees of American courts in the matter of anti-trust policy, and with respect to American balance of payments policy.
In each case, the report put forward recommendations that would create Canadian law and administrative agencies that would attempt to nullify and countervail the American intrusion. United States law and policy forbid, in effect, American firms and their subsidiaries to trade with nations designated as enemies-Mainland China, North Viet Nam, North Korea and Cuba. The report recommends that Canada create a government export trade agency to oversee such Canadian trade with these countries as is consistent with Canadian foreign policy, and, as a last resort, require American controlled firms to fill bona fide orders which would otherwise be lost to Canada.
One of the approaches taken to extraterritoriality is the setting up of an export trade agency to take care of the problem that has confronted Canadian subsidiaries of United States parents in regard to trading with the enemy legislation and so forth.
The approach to branch plant operation can be stated in this way:
But the real issue in this regard may turn out to be whether American-controlled firms are able to enter into rationalization agreements promoted by the Canadian government. American anti-trust law may inhibit such activities on the grounds that they involve collusion between firms. In so far as rationalization programs appear to be essential if Canadian industrial efficiency is to be increased in a dramatic, but orderly way, it is important to have the Canadian interest clarified. Present rudimentary consulting arrangements between Canadian and American authorities amount to little more than the Canadian authorities being kept informed. The strengthening of these arrangements hinges on Canada articulating its interests so that they will be given greater weight by the United States. This will require a clear Canadian legal position which the American parents of Canadian subsidiaries can point to when they are asked to do things which violate American law but are desired by the Canadian government.

The issue of the application of United States balance of payments policy to the subsidiaries of American corporations has been very much alive in recent months. While the United States has been applying voluntary controls for some time, it issued new mandatory controls on direct investment just as the report was being completed. Since the report was issued, Canada has been exempted. Given the disastrous consequences of these controls for the Canadian dollar, the exemptions can only be regarded as a welcome development.
The other more important matter, Mr. Chairman, is the problem of the rationalization of Canadian industry. I think it is agreed among Canadian manufacturers that they must broaden the base of exports. At the moment we have a 65 per cent dependency on exports to the United States. As one studies the problem one feels that Canada has opted out in favour of economic integration with the United States. I think this was the main contention between the hon. Walter Gordon, who stood for nationalism, and Mr. Winters and the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, who stood for continentalism. It appears at the moment that the continental-ists have won out. One feels the gradual opting out by the government in favour of economic integration with the United States.
When one reads the speeches of the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce one feels that he simply takes as an accomplished fact that we should follow the course of economic integration. I find it quite strange that this minister, in view of the riding he represents and the province from which he comes, would accept this as almost a fait accompli.
We have also been given guide lines for the good Canadian, corporate citizen as set forth by the former minister of trade and commerce. It has been said that this approach is the Boy Scout approach to the tackling of the main problem of rationalization and the penetration of foreign investment in Canada.
The problem of rationalization, Mr. Chairman, is not an easy one. I can recall sitting as a member of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs and hearing the president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce setting forth a particular problem. This gentleman is also president of Electrohome. He said that in Canada there are nine manufacturers of television sets, seven of which are U.S. owned, the remaining two being Canadian owned, Electrohome and Clairtone.

It was part of the program of the government of the province of Nova Scotia to help the company in their financing so that they could penetrate the northeastern sector of the United States. However, they have run into difficulty, and without the aid and assistance of the government of Nova Scotia they would experience real problems.

One readily appreciates the problem of rationalization in this instance of seven U.S. owned companies and two Canadian owned companies in a rather large field of endeavour.
Turning to the automobile industry, Mr. Chairman, we in Canada are almost 100 per cent dependent on the U.S. owned automobile industry in Canada. A small country like Sweden, with less than eight million people, has been able to stake out for itself an automotive industry which has been very successful not only in Sweden but has expanded to England, France, Italy and Japan. Mr. Chairman, I have listened with considerable interest to hon. members speaking in this debate and have noted a variety of viewpoints expressed. These have all indicated the hope of increased trade, or perhaps I should say a continuing increase in an already expanding trade pattern which is very gratifying indeed.
There are those who advocate virtually unbridled free trade and those who tend to overprotect. In my opinion the answer is one of balance. This word "balance" has become a favourite of mine in recent years, and perhaps that is why I am a Liberal. Some call us a party of the middle of the road, which may be just another way of expressing balance. We in this party run the whole gamut of viewpoints, bringing about the creative tensions that result in solutions which do in fact give balance to our policies.
[The Acting Chairman (Mr. Richard).!
I might say that previously my favourite word was "dispassionate", but I do not think one can make progress, or even workable political decisions, completely devoid of passion. Here too we must seek a balance between overemotionalism and clinical objectivity. I might say that as I grow older I have an increasingly nostalgic attitude toward passion, or, as some say, "nostalgia just is not what it used to be".
I too look forward to the day when we can have true free trade. To rush into this blindly, however, would be the height of folly. It is necessary to exercise a healthy degree of economic nationalism to prepare ourselves for the increasing degree of free trade which we are currently experiencing and which we face in the future. Very much the same applies to our increasingly international society. Our internationalism must be tempered with a realistic degree of nationalism in order that we may contribute, compete, and even survive as a nation.
These are ideals to which we aspire, just as a just society is an ideal. Without such ideals we have either no purpose or a distorted purpose on which to base our present policies and actions.
I was very much impressed with the message of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance last Thursday night when he explained some facets of the results of the Kennedy round negotiations. When the machinery tariff legislation was being prepared I participated in representations by my industry to the Department of Industry and the Department of National Revenue. We were apprehensive about some aspects of this legislation and saw many possible loopholes. Since the Kennedy round reductions have been in force we have found that these apprehensions were unfounded. The proper administration of the legislation and, more important, the spirit of the legislation, have resulted in a far more favourable economic climate and the elimination of much which was distasteful in prior legislation.
My own company is engaged in the manufacture and distribution of machinery for the plastics industry, and I am aware of what have proved to be ill-founded concerns on behalf of our industry. Even so, I was pleasantly amazed to learn from the parliamentary secretary that there has not been a single complaint. This has very much affected my attitude toward the proposed anti-dumping legislation as a member of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs which is
November 19, 1968

studying it. We have tended to look at every conceivable abuse of the anti-dumping code that is possible, both by industry and by improper administration by government. In hearing the representations from industry groups I sense the same type of apprehension that existed prior to the implementation of the tariff legislation to which I previously referred.
I doubt that it is possible to draft legislation that is absolutely foolproof. If it is possible, I suspect that the result would be bad legislation, legislation so tight and so completely restrictive that it could prove negative in its implementation.
What we have in the proposed anti-dumping code is a distinct improvement over prior practices. It depends for its effectiveness on an alert business community and its intelligent discretionary interpretation and administration by the appropriate government officials. This has been demonstrated in the machinery tariffs, and I have no fear that it will be any less effective when the new anti-dumping code is implemented.
What we are dealing with is a new spirit in international trade negotiations, a spirit which gives greater opportunity while at the same time giving reasonable and necessary protection. It is true that we are somewhat vulnerable, but only if we sit back and let the legislation become more effective than our energy and our spirit of enterprise. It presents a challenge to Canadian industry to compete, but it also offers us the great opportunity to exploit export markets that were virtually denied to us previously. If we cannot survive in this new atmosphere it will only be because we do not deserve to, and if we cannot survive under this new set of conditions we will be annihilated under free trade.
The automotive trade agreement is another example of change which many feared but which is resulting in benefits to our economy that were otherwise unobtainable. This particular legislation is not without its difficulties or its dangers, and to these we must be alert. The net result to date, however, has been an unqualified gain commensurate with fairness to both countries involved. If it were not for its scale it could well be looked upon as prototype legislation, the pattern of which might be followed by other industries. It may prove to be the most desirable method of achieving free or close to free trade which we can devise and still retain our sovereignty.
Ways and Means
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The message I am trying to convey is that we, and by "we" I mean industry, labour and government, must be prepared not only to meet change but to seek it. We must look for greater opportunity, which will require greater inventiveness, imagination, skills and plain hard work. At the same time, we must exercise due and reasonable caution to make certain our legitimate self-interests are properly protected.
It is in this vein that I approach the report of the task force on the structure of Canadian Industry, familiarly known as the Watkms report. I have made only a cursory study of it and my observations are necessarily subjective, as the proprietor of a modest business largely confined to the plastics industry. My associations are overseas to a great extent, but also largely in the United States, and involve close associations with leaders of multi national companies, particularly in the chemical industry. It is with this orientation that I view the report.
I think, however, that the Watkins Report deserves serious study. My observations at this time are necessarily short and superficial. They are intended, however, to introduce and stimulate further discussion on a subject which has been much misunderstood. In Professor Watkins' own words:
If all of our proposals were put into effect, Canada would still have one of the most liberal policies toward foreign direct investment in the world. Foreign corporations should still find Canada a profitable place to invest.
I think Professor Watkins is purposely understating in this context as we would still have more liberal policies than almost any developed nation in the world, nations to which foreign capital is flowing steadily.
In my opinion, the spirit and direction of the report are not at all incompatible with maintaining the necessary climate to continue to attract foreign capital and know-how. The exception is a possible distasteful reaction to the establishment of a state trading agency to deal with communist countries in certain, well defined situations. The intent, as specifically defined in the report, however, is not without merit. It deals with licensing arrangements, amongst other things, which are frequently the easy way of doing things but which have restricted Canadian companies to the domestic market. Some method of incentives to permit export could be devised. The waiving of the withholding tax on royalties could be considered. Perhaps the production

Ways and Means
of certain items under licence for export, or export to specific markets, would prove a practical compromise. The greater the export freedom, the greater the incentive. British Commonwealth and other markets could be negotiated. In cases where the product name or design are not the major consideration, where patents or technology are the prime benefits, marketing could be done under a different trade name and with distinctive styling and the entire world market opened up including, or even excluding, the licensor's domestic market.
The report also deals with joint ventures, which I believe require particular encouragement. In many cases a Canadian distributor develops the Canadian market which is then taken over by the foreign manufacturer, who then establishes his own manufacturing facility in Canada. Frequently, the Canadian distributor seeks another similar foreign manufacturer to represent and the cycle repeats itself ad infinitum.
Where the Canadian company is competent, the foreign company should be encouraged to establish a joint venture. My company has had specific experience in this area and is currently forcing negotiations to this end with a leading United States company. The American principals, in turn, are endeavouring to acquire complete control. This could result in (a) the loss of the market by my company, (b) its acquisition by the United States company, or (c) a disassociation of the companies, with the American company establishing its own facility, possibly with government aid, and my company endeavouring to start from the beginning, engineering a new product line and attempting to compete with the one we established in the first instance.
With adequate government encouragement, this situation could be avoided. At present a Canadian company is subject only to its own position in the Canadian market, as opposed to the already established position and far greater resources of the American company.
It is particularly interesting to note that when my company attempted to get federal government assistance some years ago to establish a Canadian facility it was completely frustrated. The Department of Industry did not have an appropriate agency. The closest to such an agency was PAIT, and while its objectives are admirable, its interpretation of its function was far too narrow to be of benefit. In one instance alone this could have established a three million dollar business, two-thirds of which would have been export

and the remaining third replacing imports. This was a unique opportunity, and one which no longer exists as foreign companies have since seen and seized the opportunity in what would have been the export market. Without the export market the economics do not justify Canadian engineering for the domestic market. Thus, approximately a million dollars of imports continue and two million dollars in exports are lost.
Another area is assistance to firms in designated areas. Assistance to firms establishing or expanding in designated areas does not, I believe, differentiate between Canadian or foreign controlled companies. I think it would be beneficial to give Canadian companies some additional assistance. It may be well worth considering extending the benefits by a given percentage, maybe 50 per cent, or even 100 per cent, to companies controlled domestically. This should provide incentive for the establishment or expansion of small industries. Unfortunately, the smaller companies frequently do not have the personnel, resources, or the time to pursue the government sponsored programs.
This same problem also applies to Industrial Development Bank assistance. Skilled industrial development officers of the Department of Industry could well advise and expedite far more effectively than at present.
Then there is the matter of guide lines. Government guide lines for good corporate citizenship on the part of foreign companies in Canada are solely dependent on the good will of these companies for effective implementation. Generally they are for motherhood and against sin and are largely ignored, or only lip service is paid to them. I would urge something more effective, with emphasis on incentives rather than penalties.
It may well be worth considering appointing government liaison personnel to work closely with foreign controlled corporations in assisting them to co-operate with our guide lines policy. In the case of new companies entering Canada, they could well assist these companies in locating in this country, establishing domestic contacts and sources of supply, while being guided in the direction of good corporate behaviour.
In my own contact with senior officials of Canadian subsidiaries of foreign corporations, most of whom are Canadians, I have found them eager for more specific guide lines and requirements. Only in this way can they influence their patent companies in New York, Chicago, Minneapolis, or wherever they may

be located. These people are practical businessmen and they abide by the laws. If we do not provide more than pious platitudes, they will naturally react in a platitudinous manner.

Some time ago I suggested to the Department of Industry that benefits might well accrue to the company and economy if qualified engineering personnel could be hired to seek out areas for development. Such a program might initially involve the hiring of only one person who might well spend the first six months or a year reviewing existing products, scanning the markets, investigating customer requirements domestically and abroad for new equipment or products. The converse may also have merit. Canadian investment in non-resident foreign companies, particularly to acquire technology, markets and management, may well be worth consideration. The purpose of the visit was to determine the reason for certain inefficiencies which were developing. Following exploration it became apparent that some of the frequent failings of several generations of family management were responsible.
It is quite likely that this company could be acquired and part of its production transferred to Canada. It is engaged in the production of machinery of which Canada is a major importer. The potential of the company is sufficient to maintain the efficient operation of

the American facilities without considering export from the United States. Similar Canadian facilities such as Canadian Vickers, Canadian Machinery Company, Dominion Engineering, Sherbrooke Machineries, John Bertram and Sons, and many others, frequently operate below capacity or on a boom or bust basis.

All of this, Mr. Chairman, must include a study of our educational goals. The superior management skills of the United States are sadly lacking in this country. Top calibre graduate schools in management, as well as engineering, law, economics and other fields, are essential if we are to keep pace in a far more complex and highly technological society and economy. The federal government could set the pace by determining which of our universities are best suited to establish schools of international stature in specific disciplines and providing the necessary funds. Highest priority should be given to schools of business management.
As I said previously, these are in the nature of random comments from perhaps a narrow viewpoint. My hope is that they may help get the Watkins report off the shelves in government, academic and corporate offices and into the arena of political discussion, which is where we are now and where my hon. friend from Broadview was when he spoke.
We must avoid being overprotective in our approach. Industry does not require coddling; in fact it suffers from it. It does, in our particular Canadian economic milieu, need the proper climate and encouragement which only government can, and should, provide. As a Canadian businessman, however, I welcome the challenge of the opportunities and competition of a free and open market as long as it is on more or less equal terms.
In my short experience here we have spent a great deal of time, quite properly, discussing the problems of agriculture and fishing. Those from urban areas fully understand that all parts of this country and all aspects of its economy are interdependent. I am sure that those from non-urban areas are equally aware of this and will be equally interested. It is only in this house where one can gain this vital perspective, or I prefer to say balance.
Before concluding may I express a word of caution. We must be well aware that the problems about which I have spoken are not the fault of foreign investors. They are problems for which we can only blame ourselves. It is therefore critical to our friendships, international relations and our economy that

we do not misconstrue evidence of enlightened self-interest manifested by talk of reasonable economic nationalism. When we speak about foreign investment we are almost always thinking about American investment and American economic, as well as potential political, domination. It would be a tragic error to carry this even close to the point of anti-Americanism for we have no better friends anywhere and our present high standards of living would not have been possible without them.
In my rather extensive relationships with American businessmen I have found them warm, fair and energetic friends who exercise their own reasonable degree of self-interest, combined with a unique generosity that we should nurture and cherish. They are a more vocally patriotic people than we are, but when one explains to them our own love of country, our own social and economic aspirations, they almost always respond with understanding. Quite restrictive rules on foreign investment in countries with far less in common certainly have not deterred the irrepressible and admirable American businessmen. The danger is not from initiative abroad. The danger is from lack of initiative right here.

Mr. Chairman, when the Kennedy round of negotiations was first undertaken there were great hopes and expectations as to what might be achieved. Now that the negotiations have been concluded we can take a look at the results. I think it will be generally agreed that there have been modest though significant achievements in some areas of world trade. However, in spite of the progress that has been made I think we should take care not to overestimate the impact of the changes that have resulted from this round of negotiations. This point was made by Mr. David Slater in an article in "The Canadian Banker" of autumn, 1967, when he concluded:
One should thus be sceptical of the allegations that tariff levels on industrial products will be at very low levels after the Kennedy round agreements are in force.
These gains could be wiped out very quickly if there are any significant changes in world attitudes toward trade and trade problems. I think this fact does demonstrate the need for continuing efforts to free world trade from both the tariff and the non-tariff

November 19, 1969
Ways and Means
barriers which still impede the free movement of goods. Some of the concerns with respect to trade and the changes that are being introduced in the house at this time have already been discussed by some of my colleagues, and I do not intend to go over the same ground again. However, I would like to take two areas of concern and discuss them this afternoon. The first area is with respect to some of the concerns regarding the agricultural industry. Agriculture, of course, is very vitally concerned and interested in the Kennedy round agreements.
First of all, one development of the negotiations was the conclusion of the international grains arrangement. I think it was generally agreed that this was a distinct achievement in the field of world trade. However, in spite of this achievement and the gains made, it is now apparent and clear that there are some very serious problems with respect to world trade in grain. These problems have developed in spite of the achievements accomplished through the conclusion of the international grains arrangement. The details of some of these problems I will leave for discussion on another occasion.
I think we should also take note of the general pattern of tariff changes which has resulted from the Kennedy round, particularly with respect to the impact upon industrial products and agricultural products. Mr. David Slater, in the same article to which I referred a few moments ago, also commented on this aspect of the negotiations. Mr. Slater stated, as found on page 6 of "The Canadian Banker" of autumn, 1967:
The Kennedy round negotiated a multi-national cut in tariffs on industrial products. Aside from a new international cereals agreement and small cuts on a limited range of agricultural tariffs, little agricultural trade or protectionism was revised. A great disappointment is the failure to reduce significantly the high levels of agricultural protectionism now in the world. We shall deal almost exclusively-
Then he proceeds to deal with some of the aspects of the industrial tariff changes. Later in the same article Mr. Slater notes:
-the maze of agricultural protectionism and barriers to agricultural trade, which has been accentuated since the early 1920's, remains virtually unchanged by the Kennedy round.
In noting the tariff reductions that have been made in the field of agricultural products, we note that the United States has made some concessions. Some of them have been significant concessions. However, Canada has also made concessions in some agricultural products. Some of the changes as they affect

Canada and the United States were summed up in "Foreign Trade" of July 1, 1967, when it was stated:
Canada and the United States are providing free entry both ways for apples, turnips, maple sugar, maple syrup, certain berries, many grass and forage seeds, hay and straw. Duty reductions of 50 per cent, in parallel with the United States, are made on fresh pork and fresh carrots. In addition, out of season rates are reduced or removed on certain fresh fruits and vegetables, including brussels sprouts, corn on the cob, parsley, radishes, green onions, apricots, sour cherries and plums.
There is a distinct impression and a suspicion in some areas of the agricultural industry that Canada did not come off quite as well as it might have in its negotiations with respect to agricultural products. I have made inquiries of farm organizations in some circles to find whether a full analysis has been made anywhere of the impact of the Kennedy round negotiations on the agricultural industry. While such an analysis may exist, my own search did not turn up an adequate analysis of this matter.
There is great concern with respect to this problem because of the general state of the agricultural industry at the present time and because of concern for the impact of these changes on particular aspects of the Canadian agricultural industry or particular sectors of that industry. The fact is that the agricultural industry is concerned because we see examples of tariff changes which are being applied for on some products of importance to farm people. Most recently there has been an application for an increase in the tariff on twine, which would certainly add to farm costs. As has been noted by the National Farmers' Union, any price increase resulting from the imposition of a tariff on imported binder and baler twine would be borne solely by farmers who possess no means of passing on cost increases.
In some of the hearings in the finance, trade and economic affairs committee, which were referred to by a previous speaker, evidence was taken with respect to the proposed anti-dumping code. One area of concern with respect to the anti-dumping code was its impact on a number of agricultural products which are produced in Canada but which have to face competition from end of season surplus exports from the United States in particular. It was noted by some of the experts who were called before the committee that in fact the anti-dumping code would not help to deal with some of those deeply rooted problems within the area of the specific problem being dealt with in the anti-dumping

code. I think this illustrates some of the problems with which we have to wrestle and be concerned about.

We should note as well, Mr. Chairman, that Canada is the fourth largest exporter of agricultural products in the world. Canada, in considering its possible role with regard to the agricultural industry, has to note its position in relation to other countries in the world. This point was also discussed at the conference in Banff in January, 1966. Dr. Anderson, in summing up some of the papers presented to the conference, noted some of the points we need to keep in mind. He said:
A significant point brought out by MacEaehern was that Canada maintains an over-all comparative advantage to the rest of the world in agricultural production. There is a relatively stable advantage in a number of products which include wheat, barley, flaxseed, rapeseed, milk production, grade dairy cattle, some cheeses, tobacco, turnips and some fruit. Then there is a competitive advantage relative to the United States which varies by seasons and regions, and includes feeder and slaughter cattle, hogs, eggs, apples and potatoes.
The competitive advantage which Canada enjoys relative to the rest of the world has been reduced over the past decade or so; this change has been masked by the magnitude of the wheat exports in recent years. The gain in productivity of about 3 per cent per year has offset some of these costs but not enough to improve the net income of agriculture.
MacFarlane noted that restraints on trade account for much of the pattern of structural changes in importing countries. These restrains tend to. distort the comparative advantage of most farm products. Mr. Chairman, I wish to say something about the effect of the Kennedy round negotiations on the grain growers of western Canada. Traditionally we in that part of the country have been in favour of free trade, or one might say freer trade. I suspect the reason has been that living in the middle of a continent we have to move our products either east or west to Canadian markets and to world markets. In passing I may say that Canadian markets are very important to us. The people of Quebec, Ontario and the mari-times purchase our grains to feed their livestock and poultry. We cannot disregard the needs of people living in those trading areas because they, like us, are citizens of Canada.
As an individual I question the benefits that the Kennedy round negotiations brought to prairie farmers. If there are benefits they have yet to appear. Prior to those negotiations we had the international wheat agreement, which was working well. It included not only the so-called western nations but also the U.S.S.R., the most powerful nation behind the iron curtain.
In 1959 I sat in on the renegotiation of the I.W.A. Russia sat as an observer, and in 1962 it became a signatory to that agreement. But as a result of the Kennedy round negotiations among western nations, held under the GATT, we closed out participation by the U.S.S.R. in the international wheat agreement. As a result the U.S.S.R., one of the world's; most important wheat and grain producers, is: no longer bound by the terms, prices and trading arrangements made under the international grains arrangement, as the new agreement is called.
I watched with interest as the Kennedy round negotiations proceeded. They were slow and painful. Almost at the final point it seemed we would not reach any agreement on trade in grains. It was my impression that we moved from the international wheat agreement into the GATT negotiations largely at the insistence of the United States so that it would have access to European markets for its feed grains, a commodity as important to the United States as wheat is to Canada. But no sooner was that new agreement negotiated than the United States cut the price of its wheat exports and Canada encountered one of the toughest sales periods in a good many

Ways and Means
years. At the time the new grains arrangement was announced by the government of the day I noted it was stated that Canada had gained access to $1J billion worth of trade into the United States, but from our experience since then I doubt that our grain growers have gained very much.

In some areas such as this decisions are made which cannot be affected by a simple, ordinary tariff approach.

We have an oil policy in Canada which operates so that certain Canadian oil-producing areas will serve certain parts of Canada and other areas will serve other parts of Canada. If you purchase petroleum products for use on the farm in western Canada you pay a uniform price. I suspect this is the same in the east; the prices will be uniform there also. In other words, to use an economic term, the price is an administered one. These are the situations with which farmers must live.
A recent bulletin issued by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool states that a sufficient number of cattle are now being sold by farmers directly to packing plants to support the forecast that in the immediate future we will reach a point where there will be no longer a sufficient number going to the public yards to establish prices. Will we then have a free market, competition or free trade? I hope these things will be of concern to the Minister of Agriculture.
During the election we heard a lot of talk about national marketing boards, but I have not heard much about them since I arrived here. Let me suggest to the government that it had better be concerned about the situation facing the agricultural industry in western and eastern Canada. I assume an unhappy situation exists in eastern Canada if the delegation of farmers who took the trouble to drive two or three hundred miles on tractors to parliament hill is any indication. I have spent most of my life on a tractor and the last thing I would do would be to drive one 200

November 19, 1968
Ways and Means
miles on a highway. They are not built to travel on highways.
We must recognize this situation in developing our trade and financial policies. We have been very fortunate in Canada in that we have had lots of cheap land and a highly skilled labour force in the agricultural field. We have also had self-employed farmers who have used the technology available to them to the point that they are now actually beginning to get into trouble because of overproduction. Let me say again that we must adopt trade and financial policies which will allow these farmers to stay in business in order to continue to provide Canadians with cheap food, and they have been getting cheap food. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. members who have spoken during this debate for their contributions. I can assure them that their very interesting comments have been carefully noted.
Let me remind the committee of what the government put forward as its aims when entering the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations. I shall paraphrase the remarks of a previous minister of trade and commerce who was the minister of finance at the time he made a statement to the finance committee of the house when it was studying these resolutions in the spring of the year. There were certain broad considerations which were followed in formulating the tariff offers the government made in the Kennedy round. First of all, the government wanted to make certain that there was a reasonable over-all balance, in practical trading terms, between the tariff concessions we got and those we granted. Therefore every effort was made to obtain every worth-while tariff reduction offered by other countries but, of course, we gave no more than we got.
Second, we took account of how our tariff concessions and the export benefits we obtained could contribute to the balanced growth of the Canadian economy. We wanted particularly to help our secondary industries to break out of the confines of our small national market. This we could do by getting reductions in other countries' tariffs and by cutting the costs of producing in Canada for those new and expanding markets. That is
[Mr. Gleave.l
why our tariff cuts on raw materials, semifinished goods and on production machinery are an important part of the Kennedy round settlement for Canada.
Third, we sought and obtained a more reasonable degree of balance and reciprocity for each major sector of our economy and for each region.
Fourth, we wanted to ensure that through the Kennedy round Canadian consumers would benefit from greater international competition.
The tariff reductions consented to by Canada covered about $2.5 billion in imports, of which about $2 billion came from the United States. At the time the then minister of finance spoke, on the other hand, the export benefits obtained by Canada from its agreements with major trading partners covered, including wheat, over $3 billion of export trade. That was the current situation at the time the then minister of finance reported to the committee.
I should like to point out to the committee of ways and means that it is significant that in such markets as the United States and the European common market the average level of tariffs on manufactured goods will be below 10 per cent when the results of the Kennedy round are implemented. Because of the across the board tariff cuts made by our major trading partners, export opportunities will open up for the first time for a very wide range of Canadian manufactured goods. Let me suggest, however, that it is not only our manufacturing industry that will be in a position to gain. The scope of the negotiations was such that nearly all commodities, including the products of fisheries, agriculture, mining and the extractive industries, will be in a position to benefit from the lower tariff barriers facing our goods in the export markets.
Would you permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I could accept questions after I have completed my remarks.
The first round of cuts under the tariff changes has been in effect on a provisional basis since January 1, 1968. This has provided almost a year of experience and observation with respect to the operations of our economy and, more particularly, of Canada's international trade in conjunction with the tariff changes in question. I think we have had a chance to see what has actually been happening to our country's trade since these tariff changes came into effect on a provisional
November 19, 1968

basis on January 1 of this year. It is not just a matter of forecast or estimate; we have some definite results to look at.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I think it can be said that the results are certainly very encouraging. Last year the government set a 1968 export sales target of $12.3 billion. In a speech given by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to the Canadian Export Association on October 21, he pointed out that the Canadian export performance to date has been more than consistent with this goal. In the first nine months of 1968 our merchandise exports reached $9.9 billion, up $1.6 billion or 18.4 per cent from the same period last year. Meanwhile our imports have risen at a slower rate, by $811 million or about 10 per cent. In consequence I think we should be pleased to note that Canada is well on its way to achieving a $1 billion merchandise trade surplus this year. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce pointed out that this will be the largest favourable trade balance recorded in the post-war period. Therefore our over-all balance on current transactions, though still in a deficit position, will be much improved.
From a commodity standpoint, we can note that about two-fifths of this year's export gain consists of automative products. However, the gain is not limited, obviously, to increases in exports of automotive products. In fact, other products have also contributed importantly. These export products include copper, iron and steel, lumber and woodpulp, nickel and aluminium, petroleum and natural gas, and aircraft. I think these figures I have put on the record confirm my earlier remark that the results so far for Canada's trade since the Kennedy round changes were given effect to on a provisional basis have been most encouraging.
When the hon. member for Perth spoke on behalf of the official opposition he raised some question about the impact of these tariff changes on our trade with the United States.
I think it is important to observe that on the basis of the most recent trade statistics released by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the initial trends following the introduction of the first tariff reductions last January for Canada and the United States can be considered to be quite favourable from a Canadian point of view.
Although both our exports and imports are increasing, the increase in exports is much greater than the increase in imports. Indeed, in the first nine months of 1968 our exports to
Ways and Means
the United States were actually greater than our imports from that country. The hon. member for Perth commented on what he considered was the need for greater progress in dealing with non-tariff barriers. It would seem to me that certainly there was some progress in this very important area affecting international trade. One achievement was the negotiation of the agreement setting up an international anti-dumping code. As this committee of ways and means knows, the draft bill in the form of a white paper to implement Canada's commitment under this code in a legislative way is currently under detailed study in the finance committee of this house. I suggest that members of the house might want to reserve their more detailed comments on the proposed legislation until the committee hearings have been completed and it has been returned to the house by the finance committee.
I would also like to point out that a special committee of the GATT is working on a program of study of the remaining non-tariff barriers to determine their exact extent and nature. I believe its intention is to formulate a program for working toward their elimination. The Minister of Finance yesterday in a speech in New York pointed out that further progress in the elimination of non-tariff barriers is one of the major tasks before the trading nations of the world, a task that still has to be accomplished in large degree although, as I have said, with the agreement setting up an international anti-dumping code and the program of work of the GATT committee, I think some progress in this area has in fact come out of the negotiations for the Kennedy round.
If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment briefly on some of the points raised by hon. members who participated in this debate. The hon. member for Waterloo noted what he considered to be potential dangers in the general freeing of trade and cited as an example what he said was happening in the farm machinery industry. Yet if I understood correctly what the hon. member for Broadview was saying, he felt we were acting too cautiously and perhaps had not gone far enough in cutting tariffs. This might help to prove that the government in its negotiations has in fact achieved a proper balance in the interests of Canadian industry and workers.
The hon. member for Waterloo suggested, if I understood him correctly, that Canada will not automatically benefit through freeing of trade. I point out to the committee that the

November 19, 1968
Private Bills
government has in fact put into effect measures to help Canadian industry and workers to take advantage of opportunities created by the Kennedy round tariff negotiations. It has set up the new, special adjustment assistance program as well as the machinery program which will be formally implemented by the passage of the legislation before us. In addition, the increased efforts of the trade and commerce department are all aimed at ensuring maximum benefits for Canadian industry and workers from the opportunities provided by the Kennedy round.
As I have already pointed out to the committee, the average level of tariffs of our trading partners when the Kennedy round changes are implemented will be below 10 per cent on manufactured goods. Therefore the degree of concern expressed by the hon. member for Waterloo about the lack of opportunities for our manufactured goods in foreign markets should be lessened by the opportunities created by this general lowering of tariffs which previously stood in the way of our manufactured goods.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock?
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned for the supper hour I was attempting to respond to some of the very interesting comments that hon. members had made during the consideration of this resolution in this committee of ways and means. I believe I was saying that I thought the lowering of the tariffs of our trading partners with respect to manufactured goods would be opening new opportunities for Canada's secondary industry.
The hon. member for Waterloo made some reference to the auto pact, and I believe expressed the view that progress had not been as rapid as should have been the case. I think I should point out that there have been thousands of new jobs, and new and expanded plants created as a result of this pact. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, when he spoke to the Canadian Exporters Association a few weeks ago, said that notable progress under the automotive products agreement has been realized, but that these gains must be maintained and indeed expanded. He went on to say that two way trade has increased from $760 million in 1964 to $3.3 billion in 1967, and that this figure will be even higher by the end of this year. In the 1968 model year more than a million vehicles were manufactured in Canada, compared with only 700,000 in 1964. Canadian exports of vehicles and parts increased from a value of $123 million to more than $2 billion in the same period. Employment in the automotive industry has reflected its general expansion with the creation of some 17,000 new jobs.
The hon. member for Waterloo questioned whether recent labour contracts had resulted in meaningful wage parity. Certainly the unions representing the workers in the auto industry believe they have met with success in recent negotiations in moving toward wage parity, though it is my understanding that these moves are linked to productivity.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, as I have said, the figures demonstrate the increased employment and new and expanded plants that have
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Beehard).]
resulted from the automotive pact. Speaking personally, along with this improvement it seems to me that companies in the industry could do somewhat more than they are doing at the present time by way of giving advance notice to workers, and also to government, of technological change, so as to make it easier for workers and government departments that are attempting to assist them to adjust to the impact of that change, and to lay-offs, which in most cases are only temporary while various plant expansions are being carried out.
Perhaps I can discuss this matter at greater length on another occasion, perhaps during the estimates of the Department of Labour or Department of Manpower and Immigration. Still, it does seem to me that the government has in fact created a number of programs to assist not only industries but the workers involved to take advantage of the expanded opportunities presented by the Kennedy round tariff changes.
I have already referred to the adjustment assistance program, Mr. Chairman. We should also note new and expanded programs of the manpower department with respect to retraining and, if necessary, mobility, as well as job placement and counselling.
I believe the hon. member for Broadview spoke about views expressed in the recent Economic Council report in connection with the level of tariff cuts that the Canadian government is proposing to this parliament, to put into effect its commitments under the Kennedy round negotiations. My understanding of what the Economic Council actually said, Mr. Chairman, is that it did not seem to have definitely and firmly recommended that Canadian tariffs be reduced beyond the levels agreed to under the Kennedy round. What the council said in its fifth annual review, as reported at page 197, was that unilateral tariff reductions-and I am now quoting the report-
-perhaps in the form of an accelerated reduction of Canada's Kennedy round tariff reductions, might well be appropriate if the recent high and persistent general price and cost increases were to continue in Canada.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, such a statement is not exactly the same as a firm and definite recommendation. The hon. member for Broadview, in commenting on this point, seemed to equate effective protection with the degree to which Canadian producers can keep prices high without foreign competition. In fact, the nominal, as opposed to the effective, rate of duty on an industry's end product
November 19, 1968

places a ceiling on the price that the industry can charge for the product and I gather, still not charge more than the laid down cost of the imported product. Effective protection merely measures the extent to which the industry can increase its value added per unit of output because of the tariff structure-in other words, the extent to which it can be less efficient in processing than its foreign competitors. I am informed that Canadian levels of effective protection, at least before the Kennedy round, were not too far out of line with those of other countries such as the United States and the United Kingdom.
The hon. member for Broadview also expressed some concern at what has been said in the United States about what might be termed moves toward increased protection. We should note that the Minister of Finance, in his speech in New York yesterday, seemed in effect to caution the United States on the effect that moves toward increased protection in that country, would have on its trading relations with its neighbours and trading partners, including Canada.
The hon. member for York North made some very interesting comments and was able to base them upon his own personal experience as a manufacturer, as someone who was meeting competition in Canada from abroad and also competing with others in countries with which we trade. Certainly it is very good to hear from him as someone in the machinery industry, and to learn that he agrees that the machinery program has been working relatively smoothly.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, the hon. members for Saint-Hyacinthe, for Beauce and for Temiscamingue (Messrs. Ricard, Rodrigue, and Caouette) have dealt with the problems of the textile and shoe industries. I can assure them that the government is well aware of the problems and difficulties of those industries.
I also wish to assure them that the tariff reductions applicable to those industries are very low. For instance, for the textile industry, in general the Canadian tariff has been reduced by only 2.5 per cent and, in several cases by only .5 per cent. I must add that tariff reductions, for the shoe industry, are also very moderate. In addition, those reductions have been extended, in most cases, for a maximum period.
I believe those members also spoke of another matter, dumping, and as I have said, 29180-1861
Ways and Means
the bill that is based on the international anti-dumping agreement has been referred to the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs which is in the process of studying all the evidence of the industries affected by this bill.
We will have the opportunity of continuing our discussion on this bill when it is sent back to the house by the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs.

Now, Mr. Chairman, a number of hon. members also made comments with respect to the agricultural sector. I am informed that the agricultural package, while it can be described as being of somewhat modest size, is actually reasonably balanced between the United States and Canada. I understand that in terms of our trade with the United States we gave and received concessions on agricultural products to a trade value of about $95 million per annum each way.
With respect to the question of our sales of wheat, the minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce discussed this question in some detail when he spoke to the meeting of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool just a few days ago on November 4. I think it useful to recall that at that time he said that the government is well aware of the long, hard struggle that went into developing a system of orderly marketing under the wheat board for western Canada. This concept of orderly marketing is still valid and will continue to serve as a base for our wheat marketing policies. The principle was carried into the international sphere where it served as a basis for the international wheat agreements and now for the international grains arrangement. The other major exporters have all expressed their determination to observe the terms of the arrangement with respect to minimum prices and to achieve the objectives of the arrangement.
Finally, on this point I can say that on October 10, 1968 the International Wheat Council issued a press release in which it stated that the members of the prices review committee of the International Wheat Council representing the major exporting and importing interests declared their satisfaction with the way in which the convention had worked during this period and with the fact that the international grains agreement is an effective force in the international trade of wheat.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, let me say that the Canadian government favoured the

November 19, 1968
Ways and Means
holding of the Kennedy round tariff negotiations and participated actively in it. It worked to get the best possible results for Canada, and the government is now recommending to parliament that legislation be passed to implement these results. The original Kennedy round agreement called for legislative implementation by July 1, 1968 by the countries signing it. As we know, the government negotiated an extension to January 1, 1969, a date which is not too far away.
I would therefore commend to this committee of ways and means the passage of this resolution. I believe it would certainly help to show that Canada's attitude, along the lines of what the Minister of Finance said in New York yesterday, is not favourable to what seems to be a greater interest in protectionism on the part of some of our trading partners, and it will confirm Canada's intention to compete vigorously in international markets in a way that would help the expansion of Canada's industries. On balance, therefore, I suggest to this committee that this legislation is and will be beneficial for Canada, and I invite the house to support the passage of the resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I wished to ask the parliamentary secretary a question earlier on but he preferred to leave it to the end. I do not know if I understood his meaning correctly. As I understand him, there would be a general reduction of tariffs on Canadian commodities going into the European common market over the period of time as a result of the Kennedy round. Might I ask him what the schedule will be for the reduction of tariffs on wheat and feed grains going into the common market? In other words, what access do we have to this market in western Europe?

May I ask a supplementary question, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the Japanese market. My understanding is that as a result of the Kennedy round the United States was conceded a reduction in the tariff

on soybeans going into the Japanese market, and the tariff on Canadian rapeseed going into the Japanese market remained as it was. Can the minister tell me if this was so, and what was the concession made to the United States on soybeans?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not have available before me information about concessions won by our trading partners, but I can certainly get that information. I cannot comment directly with respect to the duty on rapeseed moving into Japan. If my recollection serves me correctly, we did win certain expanded export opportunities with respect to rapeseed. Again I would ask the hon. member's indulgence to permit me to give him a more detailed answer not only with respect to the Canadian commodity in question but with respect to the concessions won by the United States in which he is interested, and allow me to present this answer in a more detailed fashion when we are in committee of the whole house on the bill itself.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary a question. He gave some figures showing the growth in exports for the first nine months of the year. I wonder if he can give us any figures on the growth in exports to countries other than the United States.

I do not want to take up the time of the committee. The parliamentary secretary can give us this information at some other time.

I propose at this time to take up only a few minutes of the time of the committee on the first item because I can speak later on this subject as it is covered by item 40. However, I feel I am perfectly in order in referring to it now.
Some time ago the government of Prince Edward Island formed a delegation to come to Ottawa to speak to the federal cabinet and particularly to the Prime Minister to impress on the government the need for the construction of a permanent link between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I believe the delegation demonstrated conclusively that in the long run the building of a permanent link would be in the national interest and the most economic course to follow, bearing in mind the projected cost over the years ahead of maintaining the present service. Just as important, perhaps, they impressed on the federal government the need for making a decision at the earliest feasible date. It is of course understandable that the government of Prince Edward Island will be placed at a disadvantage in its planning for the future if it does not know what decision the federal government will reach with regard to this proposed transportation link.
This is a subject which is of tremendous importance to the inhabitants of Prince Edward Island. People in other parts of Canada may not fully appreciate how vital it is; in some areas it may be considered that the estimated expenditure is extremely high in relation to the population concerned, and so on. I should like to point out that this is a project which would be of benefit not only to Prince Edward Islanders, although it would be of great economic value to that province, but to all Canadians who travel to Prince Edward Island, especially during the tourist season. As a matter of fact the great congestion which occurs during the summer months is occasioned chiefly by visitors from other parts who wish to make this trip.
Supply-Public Works
I suggested that the estimated cost might seem extremely high in relation to the population concerned. However, we should bear in mind that the cost of government generally is high. The federal government is now spending yearly about half as much as this causeway will cost for this number of people in every part of Canada, so what Prince Edward Island is asking is that over a period of years the federal government designate for the building of a causeway about twice the annual expenditure that it expends on this number of people in all parts of Canada.
Ever since confederation, transportation has been a subject of such importance that islanders generally consider this project to be a matter of top priority as far as federal expenditure is concerned. This view is not limited to those who live on the island. Perhaps I might read into the record a telegram which was recently sent to the government by the Maritimes Transportation Commission. It is dated November 7, 1968, and reads as follows:
Maritimes Transportation Commission directors meeting in Moncton yesterday expressed concern over possible indefinite postponement of or outright cancellation of the construction of a permanent link between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.' This commission reiterates its position that permanent link is imperative to reduce costs of transport and to overcome increasing delays hindering the movement of products and people between the island province and the mainland. Over its more than forty year history this commission has been constantly aware of difficulties of traversing the Northumberland strait_
difficulties which have frustrated and, without a permanent link, will continue to frustrate the economic development of the province. Even with increased ferry service in recent years and with planned improvements at terminals which this commission welcomes, no solution short of a permanent link will solve the delays and costs incurred by tourists, businessmen and trade and commerce travelling to and from Prince Edward Island. The Maritimes Transportation Commission endorses the principles of the brief presented by the government of Prince Edward Island to you and your colleagues recently relative to the construction of a permanent link and we urge your government to take immediate and effective action to bring about within a reasonably prompt period the completion of the Northumberland crossing project in which 12 million dollars have already been invested.
J. M. Crosby, Chairman,
Maritimes Transportation Commission
I think most Prince Edward Islanders agree completely with the sentiments expressed in this telegram.

Mr. Chairman, with brevity, but with the utmost sincerity, I would like to support the arguments which have been marshalled by my colleague, the hon. member for Malpeque. If I do not speak at length, it is not that I am not deeply concerned about this project. Indeed, it is because I have been so deeply concerned, like my colleague, that I have been discussing it for a good many years in this parliament and elsewhere.
I, too, am hopeful that the minister, who is I believe a minister who has some understanding of national problems, will see the compelling urgency of this project being put forward.
We all know that in our part of Canada the economic situation vis-a-vis the rest of Canada is not very hopeful, and the only way to make it more hopeful is of course to make a rational assault upon those things which put us at an economic disadvantage. As all the experts and certainly all the public men for many years have realized, one of the great disadvantages which our part of Canada has undergone and borne, as this country was created in its peculiar nature, is the problem of transportation; and the four provinces, the maritime provinces, are the ones which have the greatest and most acute economic pains from their transportation difficulties.

We have watched and studied with a good deal of concern statistics, studies from the Economic Council of Canada and the Dominion Bureau of Statistics about the widening prosperity gap. It is terribly important that our produce, our fine agricultural produce, and our excellent products of the sea should get to their markets as quickly as possible. It is extremely important that our most expandable and expansive industry, namely tourism, be furthered in every possible way. There are now about a million people coming to Prince Edward Island every year. It is a direct loss of revenue when any people find that delays in the ferry transportation cause them to turn away to some other province, very nice but not quite so nice, like New Brunswick or Nova Scotia.
I think, apart from all the arguments which have been marshalled before this government, and by our premier-and I support everything he and his cabinet said-as my colleague suggested, and indeed underscored, it is sound economy to build this permanent link and build it as quickly as possible. I know of no bridge, highway or turnpike which has upon it a reasonable toll, in an area where there is much traffic, that is not self-amortizing, usually in a time shorter than those who created the structure predicted.
The cost of maintaining the ferries is increasing. It is escalating year after year. The more traffic and people, the greater is the total cost and the greater the per unit cost. Therefore the soundest economic solution, a permanent crossing, is what is needed at the present time. I agree with my colleague when he says we are delighted with the new boat, but we do note it has been announced that two of the existing ferries will be withdrawn from service. So we get one and we lose two.
We can project that there will be a heavy increase in traffic, so I would say to the minister that this is not only something that Prince Edward Island wants-of course it does,-but it would be one forward step which to a degree would cope with the economic disparity which our part of Canada suffers. We know, Mr. Chairman, that no country can be truly prosperous if any region thereof is lagging behind the national average in those economic facts of life which make for the good society and for the just society, so with all the urgency I could command I recommend to the minister a quick move on this measure.
