Mr. Chairman, in dealing with the estimates of the Department of Public Works I would begin by saying that there are in the constituency of Churchill a number of projects which come within the jurisdiction of this department. However, there is one area which is at the present time waiting anxiously for a decision for the department. I refer of course to the town of Churchill. The people who live in Churchill are waiting to see what will happen with regard to their desire for redevelopment of the townsite.
It is interesting to know that for a number of years, I would say possibly since 1959, the federal Department of Public Works has been more or less designated as being in charge of the future developmentof the Churchill peninsula. The people living there are extremely anxious to learn the proposals the minister's department is going to offer to cabinet in relation to this development.
As the minister knows, Churchill is made up mainly of federal government employees, National Harbours Board employees, Department of Public Works employees and Canadian National Railways employees. Therefore it has been felt by previous governments, and I hope by this government, that at least 75 per cent of the obligation for the development of the townsite of Churchill falls upon the federal government. Many people who have followed with interest the problems of the people of Churchill often wonder why these people who are living within a community inside a province feel that the federal government has an obligation on their behalf to provide services which are normally provided by a municipality, town or city. However, Churchill happens to be in a vastly different category because were it not for mainly federal government establishments there would be no community whatsoever, apart from possibly a few native people. It is admitted, of course, that there are at Churchill a number of provincial government employees.

However, if one were to take a census I am sure he would find that something over 75 per cent of the people in Churchill are there as a result of federal government establishments. Before I make a plea to the minister with regard to the plans of the federal government for the development of Churchill, I should like to say that the people feel there are certain things they are desirous of having. I refer to such things as new land areas available, private ownership of housing and a full business development. They are interested also in consideration being given to the site of Fort Churchill being brought within the boundaries of the town for taxation purposes. I believe the minister and his officials should give serious consideration to a gradual withdrawal from some consumer services, thus permitting a gradual takeover by private enterprise. I believe the Murray B. Jones report recommended this procedure and suggested the new business tax revenues would augment the residential property taxes revenue.
There was a period of time when National Defence was strongly entrenched at Fort Churchill. A number of commercial services built up as a result, and at that time possibly they were necessary. However I would say that with the phasing out of the military establishment at Fort Churchill and the replacement of the personnel by public works employees, it now seems as though a careful look should be taken at the possibility of gradual withdrawal of some of the services which are available to the people, so that private enterprise could take over. Some of the areas which I suggest could be taken over by private enterprise would be structural contracting, probably transport services, vehicle maintenance, plumbing and electrical contracting, painting and possibly laundering and cleaning services. These could very easily be carried out by private enterprise. The people of Churchill have felt this way for some time, and I am sure there are a number of people there who would be willing to invest money in these various businesses.
The ironical part about the situation is that it seems many of the federal employees who have been transplanted into Churchill have gradually taken over the operation of some of these services. I must say that I have not seen evidence of a takeover by federal employees in all the fields I have mentioned, but in many cases federal employees have taken over some of these services. If they are being

provided with facilities to operate these services at nominal sums on government property, you can understand the consternation this creates amongst people who would like to operate these services in the townsite of Churchill.
I plead with the minister for an early decision by his department on some of the recommendations of the Murray B. Jones report. This report was developed partly as a result of the efforts of the federal government under C.M.H.C., through the co-operation of the province of Manitoba. However, I believe the people of Churchill contributed some 12.5 per cent of the cost of making the report.
There have been many reports over the years concerning the possible development of the townsite of Churchill. For some reason or other, these reports have never resulted in any development whatever. Some eight years ago, at a time when the Department of National Defence had an establishment in Churchill, a plan was presented by the federal government for the development of a new townsite some five miles removed from the present one. Unfortunately, but possibly for justifiable reasons, this plan was not accepted by the people of Churchill. Shortly after that, the military base was phased out, and for the last five years relatively no encouragement has been given to the people of Churchill to expect that there would be a development of their townsite. I know all the reports have suggested quite substantial outlays of money in relation to the development of this town-site. However, I believe I can speak on behalf of the people and tell the minister that, while consideration may be given to a plan to develop the town, if some means could be found to provide the people with sewer and water systems within the present townsite I am quite sure they would be willing to wait a little longer, until a complete development plan could be agreed upon by the federal and provincial governments.
I am certainly not casting any criticism the minister's way when I say this, but I know from discussions with him that he feels one of the things Churchill should do is become incorporated. Many people have this idea. The people of Churchill themselves have considered the possibility on many occasions, but for reasons of their own they have decided not to become incorporated. I only hope that the minister, in looking over the possibilities and the recommendations of the Murray B. Jones report, will not come to the conclusion that nothing can be done for the town of

Churchill unless it becomes incorporated. I can assure him that if he does this, all he will be doing will be handing the ball back to the people of Churchill. He will be saying: Until you become incorporated, we have no further responsibility.
I would ask the minister to take particular note of the words of the Prime Minister on October 28 when, in my opinion, he accepted responsibility for the federal government. The Prime Minister stated, as reported at page 2090 of Hansard:
After having met the premier of Manitoba, there was an exchange of correspondence. I wrote to him indicating that certain proposals that had been made by him were under review by us-
I do want to make it clear that the ball is now in our court and that the cabinet will be receiving from the Minister of Public Works very soon according to my information proposals about measures that can be taken with regard to the city of Churchill.
He advanced Churchill to the status of a city in quick order. I am sure the people of Churchill would be very pleased to remain a community, provided they can get the services for which they are not only asking but which I feel they are justified in having.

The Prime Minister went on to say:
I hope nothing in my previous answer left the impression that we were waiting for the government of Manitoba to act. I want to make it clear we hope to come forth with some proposal very soon.

The researchers excuse themselves; the fault is not theirs but, doubtless, according to some employees of the research section, that of the department or of some of the employees of the Public Works Department.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to specify that I am not blaming the situation on the minister himself; I know he has other things to attend to, but I should like to ask him, expressly, to order an inquiry in his department as soon as possible in order to find out why his officials refuse, knowingly, to give replies to hon. members.
I think that no matter what party any member belongs to, he has the right to know what the government is planning to do or is doing in his riding and for this reason the Minister of Public Works should have an inquiry made in his department so that in future his department will give the same close co-operation as the other departments give to

the research service set up to inform all members.
Mr. Chairman, I think that it is essential before we consider statistics and shuffle through many projects which are in many cases very desirable-and as I said earlier in my speech, I do not want to deal with particular points-to bring up this point so that the minister will see to it that some changes are brought to this factual situation which is completely unacceptable.
Before concluding my remarks, I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the great needs of the riding of Lotbiniere, and particularly to those of the region of Bois-Francs, in order that a federal buildnig might be constructed in the very dynamic municipality of Victoriaville. The need is urgent. At the present time, the offices of the Manpower Centre are perched, so to speak, on the third floor of the Victoriaville post office which- although I do not mean to compete with the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Ca-ouette), who said the other day that a post office in his riding looked like a hen house- looks like a hundred year old hen house.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to bother the minister about this. I know he takes it seriously. As a matter of fact, whenever I have raised the question with him, he has considered it carefully. I wish to tell him we are getting impatient, especially the people in the riding of Lotbiniere and in the area of Bois-Francs, and we are awaiting a favourable answer from him because we would like to know exactly where things stand concerning the construction of a public building in Victoriaville.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask again the minister to order a complete inquiry among officials of his department, so that in future those officials will no longer refuse to supply information which is not absolutely confidential, and to which members are entitled, regardless of their party affiliation, in order to do a better job and to inform their constituents.
I shall therefore hope to receive soon in my office the answer of the minister to the request I have presented to him, and I hope that the officials in the gallery are listening attentively and that they will refresh the minister's memory. I think that all hon. members will recognize that we have a right to be informed and that this right must prevail over the interests of civil servants.
November 19, 1968

Mr. Chairman, I rise
merely to say a few words by way of support for the arguments advanced by several hon. members opposite respecting the necessity of the Northumberland causeway to Prince Edward Island. While these hon. members have presented the case for the causeway very well, it might be useful if support from both sides of the house were indicated for this very important project.
I think we all realize that Prince Edward Island is one of the poorest areas of the country, in terms of its possibilities for industrial development. It may be that at some stage in the future oil will be discovered. Companies have searched there before for this valuable product. It may be that great industrial complexes will be built up, but this does not seem within the realm of reasonable expectation. What would seem to be more likely is that advantage could be taken of those resources that are naturally already there, and these resources are principally in the areas of farming, fishing and the tourist industry.
I would like to take the tourist industry as an example of the development problem the Island faces. All those of us who have waited in the long line at either Cape Tormentine or Borden know of the wait of five, six, or seven hours which may occur before ferry space is available to take one across. There is no doubt that this is not only a factor which makes the life of the tourist going to or from Prince Edward Island more difficult, but it is also one which inhibits the tourist trade both by reputation and by experience. On almost any summer day one can sit there in a car and see a number of other cars leaving the line because the people are no longer willing to wait. It has been estimated in a survey conducted by the Stanford Institute that the tourist capacity of P.E.I. could easily be some 3.6 million tourists, and yet at the present time facilities are able to take over only some 400,000 tourists a year. If we were going to have enough ferries to carry the maximum number of tourists across, instead of the four ferries which we have had during recent years in active service, we would have to build 32 ferries at a cost of some $14 million per ferry. According to my calculations this amounts to more than the highest estimate of the cost of the causeway. I present this merely as an example of the potential for development if this valuable transportation link were built.
Supply-Public Works
This is not merely a matter of importance to those people who happen to be citizens of Prince Edward Island, or even to those who happen to want to visit there to spend part of their summer on the beautiful beaches of that fair isle. It seems to me it is important to all the people of Canada to aid in the development of this province, rather than continuing in the tradition of handouts. It is important to aid in the development of those resources which are naturally there, which are those that can most adequately be built upon by aid from the federal government.

Mr. Chairman, I would not want anything I have to say to be misconstrued as being critical of the minister, either personally or in the carrying out of his duties to date. I want to say also however that it is difficult to be too critical of the policies of the Department of Public Works as they have been carried out in the past two or three years.
I begin my remarks by saying that, like my colleague from Vancouver East, I want to make some reference to the notion of planning in the minds of those responsible for this department. It is pretty difficult to understand what possible notion of planning this department can have when it succeeds in bringing before us estimates calling for over $40 million in the construction of buildings here in the capital city area alone, at the very time when costs have risen to an all time high-the cost of money, the cost of land and other factors. We look at the estimates and we see an appropriation of over $41 million for the construction of office space and buildings in the capital region, and an appropriation requested of something like $16 million for rental which, I take it, is for rental of space in buildings. Last year the former member for Carleton, Mr. Bell, and I filed questions on the order paper having 10 or 12 parts to them, in an effort to get information from the department as to what their building or office space rental policy was.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
We sought to ascertain how much they were paying per square foot, whether the department had agreed to lease space before construction began, and so on. More than five months elapsed and eventually the house was dissolved; the answers to these questions were never provided by the department. I am glad to see that an hon. member of the Conservative party has re-filed a lengthy question

November 19, 19G8
Supply-Public Works
on the subject of departmental building practices. I hope the minister will take the time necessary to check into what the department has been doing in connection with rental policy. I am informed on fairly good authority that there has been a slip-shod and neglectful approach to the renting of space-that whole floors of newly constructed, privately owned buildings have been leased by the department at high rents, and then allowed to go unused for months. I am told that after being vacant for several months-and this is space for which $5.85 a square foot is being paid-staff would be brought into this accommodation, but not in sufficient numbers to make complete use of it-a space intended for 35 or 40 people would be used by only 10 or 12.
On October 1 of this year an article appeared in one of the Ottawa papers about departmental policy with respect to building construction. According to this article the Department of Public Works had somehow changed its thinking, and has decided to pay more regard to suitability for function than to the notion of prestige in connection with office buildings. If this is so, it is a welcome development and I should like to think that the new Minister of Public Works has something to do with this change in outlook. We are offered, as an example, a set of figures relating to the Department of National Health and Welfare Building at Tunney's Pasture. Judy's tower, it was called. This was to have cost $10 million for 18 floors 220 feet high. Since then, apparently, even though construction costs have risen, it has been possible for the department to estimate that it can be built to 23 floors, 30 feet higher overall, for $3 million less.
If this is the result of applying the policy of suitability for use, rather than prestige, I pray that the department will stick to its guns and follow this new policy. If it can get more space for less money, if it can build for $16 a square foot instead of $23 let us have more of it. But I know that the department must be under pressure from other departments of government to slip in a few extras so as to provide a building with a prestige image. Maybe a time will come when the government can afford prestige buildings. But that time is certainly not now, when we seem to be encountering all kinds of economic and financial difficulties, when the government is under pressure from the provinces and from many other quarters to embark upon increased expenditure. Here is one area in which money can be saved. So far it has not been considered. The health and welfare

building at Tunney's Pasture is one example. The National Arts Centre is another. The example now being set by some ministers of the crown also leaves a great deal to be desired.
At a time when the government cannot find enough money to raise the pensions of superannuated civil servants there is something obscene about pouring $46 million into a National Arts Centre, and about providing office space for cabinet ministers which one does not measure by the square foot but by the acre, complete with luxurious carpeting, expensive wood panelling, coloured telephones and all that kind of nonsense. Who needs it, except perhaps ministers with a more than usually developed egotistical sense? I know this does not apply to the Minister of Public Works, and I hope he will see to it that the Department of Public Works is able to resist pressures for prestige office space and prestige office buildings.
It is my understanding that the Department of External Affairs is to have a new building soon. This is a senior department and I would be very surprised if it did not attempt to use seniority and muscle to get a prestige building. The argument will be that such a building is necessary in order to give an impressive image to visitors from foreign countries. I suggest this is a poor argument. If Canada wishes to impress people from other countries it could best do so by providing more in the way of foreign aid. We are a young country with a great future, and we should be prepared to do more to help less fortunate nations. There should be no need to resort to such artificial things as prestige, connected somehow with office buildings and their appointments.
There is something basically unfair about spending more than $40 million on office space here in the capital at a time when it is difficult to find money for very necessary public works in other regions of this country. The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville referred to the need to build a causeway for Prince Edward Island. The hon. member for Vancouver East complained of the extreme difficulty of access to the airport at Vancouver. Many other examples could be given. In my own riding there is a crummy old bridge which can only be used under restriction because the department cannot find a couple of hundred thousand dollars to get it fixed. The industry of the area, which depends on trucking, has been placed at a disadvantage for two years because trucks have to be re-routed for 15 or 20 miles, and

this will continue as long as this crummy old bridge stays unrepaired.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I do not know how many studies have been made. The department has tested it on a number of occasions. Its first finding was correct. The eastern approach to the bridge was weak and unable to support heavy loads hitting the ramp at high speeds and so the weight restriction was imposed. But one would hope that after the passage of a year there would be some definite indication that at least there would be a timetable for repair of this bridge. However, there has been nothing of the sort. My latest information, provided by the minister himself, is that the federal government is not going to negotiate with the province of Manitoba to see about cost sharing this bridge over the St. Andrews lock and dam. This is a federal structure and has been so since about 1910. But although this would cost only a few hundred thousands of dollars, or thereabouts, to the federal government in cost sharing with the province, I point out that up to this point in time the federal government is pouring money by the millions into projects which, instead of being built and conceived in terms of function and use, have all too often been thought of in terms of prestige and glamour, and of satisfying the ego of some of those who occupy the buildings in question.
I wish to tell the minister that no one expects him to come before the standing committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts to tell the committee how it was that the initial estimate of $18 million for the construction of the arts centre in Ottawa somehow escalated upward to $46 million or $47 million in the end. He was not the Minister of Public Works at the time the difficulties were experienced. But I wish to tell the minister that his immediate predecessor in office, who was invited by the committee to appear before it in order to give an outline of the sequence of events that led up to this drastic increase in the cost of construction, does not want to come before the committee. He is invoking some rule of parliamentary precedent, but I think that some of these days we should ask the house for unanimous consent to allow the former minister of public works to appear before that committee in order to give us the facts.
It is not fair to expect the deputy minister of public works to answer all of the questions inasmuch as in the end the matter comes down to certain policy decisions taken in the
Supply-Public Works
department. How in fairness can the minister, or rather his predecessor, expect the deputy minister to be in a position to answer questions in that respect? This was the experience in the committee.
The basic question is that the costs escalated from $18 million to $46 million. On four or five separate occasions it was necessary to go before Treasury Board to get approval for upward cost revisions. Who made these decisions? Who recommended to Treasury Board that all this be approved? We cannot get the final answer because the minister who was up to his neck in that whole matter will not say, and he will not come before the committee.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a quick reference to one other item. It has to do with the matter of river bank stabilization. To my surprise I found that the federal government shares the cost, and sometimes pays 100 per cent of the cost of river bank stabilization, even if the work involved be undertaken to protect privately owned property against river bank erosion or slippage.
I am not quarreling with the principle of whether or not the federal government should pay out money to protect the banks of rivers running along the front of property that is privately owned. I am not quarreling with that for the moment; but I do wish to say that for the past five years I have been unable to get any clear indication of the criteria that go into the decision making by the department as to what particular application for federal cost sharing for river bank stabilization will be approved or not.
Quite often one or another province, one or another municipality within a province, jointly or separately will make application to the Department of Public Works for cost sharing to shore up and stabilize river banks involving private property and sometimes municipal property. From my experience to date the federal government has not shown any easy inclination or quick intention to get involved in that kind of expenditure. Yet according to a return furnished in reply to an order of this house just a few days ago I found that in fact the federal government had disbursed sums in the amount of several hundreds of thousands of dollars to help pay for, and in some cases totally pay for the cost of such river bank stabilization work.
I know that the minister, when he was minister of Indian affairs and northern development, was in the habit of answering some of the questions asked and criticisms made during discussion of estimates, by letter. I

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion hope in this case he will give some indication as to the standards or criteria which lie behind the decision taken by the Department of Public Works as to whether or not a particular application for river bank stabilization cost sharing will be accepted.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, in many ways this is a rather mundane subject to raise during consideration of the estimates, but when one looks at the estimates and sees how the Department of Public Works over the past few years has spent money with abandon in many instances, one need not apologize for trying to find out why it is so hard to get a few thousand dollars, or a few hundreds of thousands of dollars to do some needed public work in some other region of the country removed from the national capital. I hope the present minister will be more responsive to the requests made of the Department of Public Works by provinces in the east and in the west, and show a little less solicitude for prestige building here in Ottawa.

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-COMPENSATION FOR INNOCENT VICTIMS OF CRIMINAL ACTS
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-COMPENSATION FOR INNOCENT VICTIMS OF CRIMINAL ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 4 I directed the following question to the Minister of Justice:
In view of the rejection by the law enforcement board of Ontario of a claim for compensation by the dependant mother and survivors of Larry Botrie, the Toronto cab driver who was killed by a criminal recently, is it the intention of the government to introduce legislation during this session to compensate innocent victims of criminal acts?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, for the moment I think the definitive word on that subject was pronounced by my colleague, the Solicitor General before the committee on justice and legal affairs.
When the same question was referred to the Solicitor General he indicated that it was not the intention of the government to bring forward legislation at this session.
I should like for a few minutes to refer to the particular case of Larry Botrie. This was a young Lebanese man who came to Toronto eight years ago and worked with his brother as a taxi driver. In the month of April this year he picked up three young passengers aged 23, 15 and 14. They told him that they wanted to go out of town, when in fact they planned to tie him to a tree on a lonely road and steal his money and his car. On Yonge Street, north of highway 401, Botrie became suspicious of his passengers and asked to be paid in advance. When they refused he turned into a Shell gas station, telling his passengers he was going to call the police. In the front seat the 15 year old pulled a bread knife from under his jacket, held it against Botrie's chest and told him to drive on. At the same time the 15 year old yelled to the 23 year old passenger in the back to get the gun which was hidden in the rear seat.
Botrie pulled the knife from the hand of the 15 year old, jumped out of the car and shouted to the gas attendant "Get the police".
November 19, 1968

Boyd, the passenger in the back seat, pulled the trigger of the gun and Botrie fell to the ground. When he was on the ground and began to crawl he was shot twice and killed. Shortly a police sergeant arrived and faced the same gun of Boyd that had killed Botrie. The sergeant took out his gun and shot and killed Boyd.
When Larry Botrie came to Canada he worked as a cab driver and sent some $35 a month to his widowed mother in Lebanon. It cost $4,000 to ship his body home. In early November this year a provincial agency, the Law Enforcement Compensation Board, heard a claim for compensation for Larry Botrie's dependant mother, and his survivors who paid the funeral expenses. The board rejected the claim on the narrow ground that the act says compensation will be paid for any person killed or injured in or resulting from assistance given a policeman in making an arrest or in keeping the peace. In other words, it is necessary that assistance be given the police while a policeman is on the scene; he must be there. On that narrow ground the board rejected the claim.
You will note that the legislation is not in respect of compensation for innocent victims of a crime. This is the reason I asked whether the government intends to bring forward immediate legislation to compensate the victims of criminal acts. It is no answer to say that this is a provincial matter because it falls within the area of law enforcement and therefore is not a federal responsibility. I should like to remind the house that the R.C.M.P. has a contract of law enforcement in all provinces of Canada, with the exception of Ontario and Quebec. There is no reason that there should not be included in that contractual obligation a provision by which there would be compensation for victims of criminal acts of violence.
At the last session the hon. member for York-Humber brought forward a private members motion recommending that a compensation board be set up to help innocent victims. The principle of the motion was accepted by the government and the matter was referred to the committee on justice and legal affairs, before which experts appeared and gave evidence with regard to other acts in other jurisdictions. I could rightly say that there was general agreement with regard to the principle. What has happened? The federal government has taken no action. In the meantime two provinces of Canada, Saskatchewan and Ontario, have brought forward legislation.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The Ontario act is far too narrow and really does not solve the problem in respect of compensating the innocent victims of criminal acts. The Saskatchewan act is a much better one, which brings together the wisdom and the experience gained from the existence of acts in other jurisdictions.
What is going to happen? If we leave this to the provinces we are going to have a hodgepodge of different acts across the country, with differences concerning jurisdiction, the type of acts giving compensation, and differences with regard to the amount of compensation. The result will be that Canadians by and large will not be treated fairly in respect of this serious problem.
What we need is a federal act embracing the best legislation, based on the experience of other jurisdictions, notably England, New Zealand, California and New York, all of which have had working experience with this type of problem. We owe it to the memory of Larry Botrie and all other citizens-

The desire to improve our laws must be accompanied, more specially in the case of the party in power, by a concern for preparing laws which are constitutional. CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- UNION DISPUTE RESPECTING REPORTING OF OTTAWA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my appearance on the late show arises from a situation which developed as a result of the dominion-provincial conference held in two areas in Ottawa a number of days ago. The C.B.C. had assigned one Ron La-plante from the province of Quebec to come to Ottawa and record a part of the proceedings, but because of a jurisdictional dispute between two unions his copy was treated as hot copy, and he could not make his reports.
This situation has many ramifications, a good number of which distressed me. I do not believe in seven minutes I could deal with all the distressing points, and I certainly do not think I could resolve the jurisdictional dispute between the labour groups, because I am not aware of all the facts. The situation which took place then I am sure could take place again and again. Because I do have good information that the situation as it existed then has not been resolved, I thought it would be worth while to present this matter to the house during the squawk show this evening.
e (10:10 p.m.)
I was a member of the committee of the House of Commons which dealt with Bill C-186 during the last session of parliament. I know how I and other members of the committee agonized over the problems of seeing that working people were represented by the labour union that they felt best could serve their interests. I know that we also had many discussions in that committee about the dangers, if national bargaining units were broken down into regional bargaining units, and where this would lead us. Even without the benefit of Bill C-186 perhaps we now have our answer in what happened with regard to our national broadcasting system as it attempted to report on this dominion-provincial conference in Ottawa. Therefore I feel that in the public interest this matter should be raised here.
There is of course the issue of freedom of the press and the public's right to know, and our rights as people in a nation not to be hurt or hindered in our knowledge by regional battles. I do not know whether Mr. Laplante, for example, was brought in to present a particular point of view, the Quebec government's point of view, let us say. He must

have been there at the request or order of management for some particular purpose which would have helped each one of us understand a little more about that conference.
If this sort of incident were repeated, one could foresee that planes would be grounded in Montreal on their way from good old Halifax to good old Ottawa because the stewardess on the Montreal to Ottawa run carries lemonade as efficiently but wears a different union label, say, than the pilot on the plane. That sort of situation of course would be ridiculous, but I suggest hardly more ridiculous than what I know of the incident I have mentioned.
I do not think we can build a nation when there is a possibility that squabbles between groups, who one might think would have the same interest but are really competing with each other, would result in the action that was taken in this particular case. I know from newsmen-and I used to be a newsman-that the battle for the union in Montreal was a very hard fought one. I know there are probably some scars left by it that will be around for a long, long time. But the fact is I very seriously question that the sort of thing that happened in the Laplante incident should have happened, and I would like some assurance in this respect. I suppose the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Stanbury) will answer, but I really think it is more a matter within the purview of the labour department. On behalf of the Canadian people we would like some assurance that this sort of thing is not apt to happen again.
